problem: What is the general solution to the equation  $\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}?$  Assume that $n$ is an integer.

feedback.problem: In degrees, what is the general solution to the equation $\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\frac{1}{2}?$  Assume that $n$ is an integer.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we find the principal value:

$$
{x}_{1}=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-\frac{1}{2})=-{30}^{∘}
$$

Our first solution lies in the $4$th quadrant and has a reference angle of ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$ Since $\operatorname{sin}⁡x<0,$ the second solution must lie in the third quadrant, and it also has ${\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13979076/assets/b3c523e882baf0b3a105e10131091e40de686b4c1483f46e7bdc235e30743a6d.png)

Since the second solution ${x}_{2}$  lies in the $3$rd quadrant, we can find it using the reference angle as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{30}^{∘} \\  & ={210}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution for the given equation is

$$
x=-{30}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘},\,x={210}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}.
$$

Writing this as $x={\theta }^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘},$ where $\theta \in [0,360),$ we get

$$
x={210}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘},\,x={330}^{∘}+n\cdot {360}^{∘}.
$$
